title: Arrow all the way from the remote database
description: Any [ADBC](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/)-capable database becomes a table source in DuckDB, with [Apache Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org/)'s columnar wire format end-to-end — no row conversions, no driver-specific glue.

sections.title: What is ADBC?
sections.description: [Arrow Database Connectivity](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/) is a database-client API standard from the [Apache Arrow](https://arrow.apache.org/) project that moves data as Arrow [columnar batches](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Columnar.html) all the way from the database engine to your query. Where [ODBC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/odbc/reference/odbc-overview) and [JDBC](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/jdbc/) convert rows on each side of the wire, ADBC keeps the columnar layout end-to-end.

bulletPoints.label: Standard API, many drivers
bulletPoints.description: [Drivers](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/current/driver/) exist for [SQLite](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/current/driver/sqlite.html), [PostgreSQL](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/current/driver/postgresql.html), [Snowflake](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/current/driver/snowflake.html), [BigQuery](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/current/driver/bigquery.html), [Flight SQL](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/current/driver/flight_sql.html), DuckDB itself, and a growing list of others — anywhere data already lives in or near Arrow.

bulletPoints.label: No row-format intermediate
bulletPoints.description: Result batches arrive as Arrow [record batches](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Columnar.html#format-record-batches) and feed straight into DuckDB's [vectorized executor](https://duckdb.org/2021/06/25/querying-parquet.html#vectorized-execution) without transposition or per-row allocation. A batch is a contiguous block of columns the driver hands DuckDB by pointer; DuckDB reads it in place.

bulletPoints.label: Pluggable driver model
bulletPoints.description: Drivers are loaded as shared libraries (or via lightweight [`manifest.toml`](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/current/driver/installation.html#manifests) files) at runtime — no recompiling DuckDB to add support for a new database.

sections.title: Two execution models
sections.description: The same ADBC machinery is reachable two ways, and the choice is architectural, not cosmetic. Both can be loaded at once against the same database.

bulletPoints.label: Catalog mode — declarative, read-only
bulletPoints.description: An [`ATTACH`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/statements/attach) mounts the remote database as a DuckDB catalog: its schemas and tables appear under an alias, and the optimizer pushes projections and filters down into the driver while streaming Arrow batches into the vectorized executor. A join against local Parquet plans as one query — `LIMIT` can short-circuit the upstream scan, exactly like reading a Parquet file. The tradeoff is that the catalog interface is **read-only** — no DDL or DML flows through it.

bulletPoints.label: Function mode — imperative, full control
bulletPoints.description: A connection handle lets you script the session explicitly: run server-side DDL/DML, set your own transaction boundaries, and perform Arrow-native bulk inserts that hand the driver columnar batches with no row-format detour. You trade automatic pushdown (here it only reaches as far as the SQL string you send) for the ability to write and to control transactions yourself.

bulletPoints.label: How to choose
bulletPoints.description: Reach for catalog mode whenever the work is read-only analytics — it's less code and the optimizer does the pushdown for you. Drop into function mode the moment you need to mutate the remote, manage transactions explicitly, or bulk-load Arrow batches in. Because both target the same driver, a common pattern is catalog mode for the queries and function mode for the occasional write, in the same session.

sections.title: Driver Setup
sections.description: ADBC drivers ship as shared libraries (`libadbc_driver_*.dylib` / `.so` / `.dll`) plus an optional [`manifest.toml`](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/current/driver/installation.html#manifests) that names the symbol to load. The extension resolves them two ways depending on how you reference the driver.

bulletPoints.label: By name (manifest-resolved)
bulletPoints.description: `'driver': 'sqlite'` looks up a `.toml` manifest in the [standard ADBC search paths](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/current/driver/installation.html#search-paths). Most install methods — [`pip install adbc-driver-postgresql`](https://pypi.org/project/adbc-driver-postgresql/), Homebrew, system packages — drop manifests in the right place automatically.

bulletPoints.label: By explicit path
bulletPoints.description: `'driver': '/path/to/libadbc_driver_xxx.dylib'` skips manifest resolution — useful for vendored drivers or unusual install locations.

bulletPoints.label: Custom search paths
bulletPoints.description: Pass `'search_paths': '/opt/adbc/drivers'` inside the connect options to add manifest directories without changing OS-level config.

bulletPoints.label: Drivers run as trusted native code
bulletPoints.description: However it's resolved, a driver loads into DuckDB's address space and runs with the user's privileges — treat it like `LOAD`. In multi-tenant or hosted DuckDB, restrict ADBC access to roles that already have arbitrary-code-execution authority, and load only [vetted upstream drivers](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/current/driver/).

sections.title: ADBC Scanner vs Airport
sections.description: Both extensions stream Arrow over the wire, but they speak different protocols and target different worlds. Use this section to pick the right tool — or load both, since they coexist cleanly.

bulletPoints.label: Use ADBC Scanner
bulletPoints.description: When the system on the other end is a database with an [ADBC driver](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/current/driver/) — SQLite, PostgreSQL, Snowflake, BigQuery, MySQL, etc. ADBC is a *client API* standard.

bulletPoints.label: Use Airport
bulletPoints.description: When the system on the other end speaks [Arrow Flight](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Flight.html) directly — typically custom services or Flight-native systems like [Dremio](https://www.dremio.com/). Flight is an *RPC protocol*, not a client API. See the [`airport`](/products/extensions/airport) extension.

bulletPoints.label: vs purpose-built scanners
bulletPoints.description: DuckDB's [`postgres_scanner`](https://duckdb.org/docs/extensions/postgres) / [`mysql_scanner`](https://duckdb.org/docs/extensions/mysql) / [`sqlite_scanner`](https://duckdb.org/docs/extensions/sqlite) are often faster for the one database they target. Reach for ADBC Scanner when no purpose-built extension exists, when you want a single client surface across many backends, or when you specifically want Arrow end-to-end (Snowflake, BigQuery).
